questions.q: Which statement best explains why the boiling temperature of the halogens increases from fluorine to iodine?

options.A: The covalent bond between the two atoms in each molecule gets stronger.
options.B: The molecules have more electrons, so the London forces between them are stronger.
options.C: The molecules become more polar, so the permanent dipole forces are stronger.
options.D: Hydrogen bonds form between the larger molecules.

questions.solution: Halogen molecules are non-polar, so the only forces between them are London forces. Down the group the molecules have more electrons, so larger temporary dipoles arise and these forces get stronger, needing more energy to overcome. (Boiling separates molecules; it does not break the \(\mathrm{X{-}X}\) covalent bond.)

questions.q: Which statement best explains why electronegativity decreases down Group 7?

options.A: The nuclear charge decreases down the group, so the bonding pair is attracted less.
options.B: The atoms have more electrons in their outer shell, so they need fewer extra electrons.
options.C: The atoms get larger and more shielded, so the bonding pair of electrons is further from the nucleus and attracted less.
options.D: The halogens become more metallic down the group, so they form positive ions.

questions.solution: Electronegativity is the power of an atom to attract the bonding pair in a covalent bond. Down the group each atom has an extra shell, so the bonding pair is further from the nucleus and better shielded from it. This outweighs the larger nuclear charge. (The nuclear charge increases down the group; every halogen has seven outer electrons.)

questions.q: Which describes iodine at room temperature?
questions.solution: Iodine is a grey-black solid that sublimes on warming to a purple vapour. Bromine is a red-brown liquid, chlorine a pale green gas and fluorine a pale yellow gas. (The physical state follows the boiling temperatures, which rise down the group.)

questions.q: Which of these mixtures reacts?

options.A: Bromine water and aqueous potassium chloride
options.B: Chlorine water and aqueous potassium iodide
options.C: Iodine solution and aqueous potassium bromide
options.D: Iodine solution and aqueous potassium chloride

questions.solution: A halogen displaces a halide ion lower in the group, because oxidising power decreases down the group. Chlorine oxidises iodide: \(\mathrm{Cl_{2} + 2I^{-} \rightarrow 2Cl^{-} + I_{2}}\). In each other mixture the halogen is below the halide in the group, so it cannot oxidise it.

questions.q: Chlorine water is added to aqueous potassium bromide. Cyclohexane is then added and the mixture is shaken and left to settle. What colour is the upper, cyclohexane layer?
questions.solution: Chlorine displaces bromine: \(\mathrm{Cl_{2} + 2Br^{-} \rightarrow 2Cl^{-} + Br_{2}}\). Bromine is more soluble in the non-polar cyclohexane, which floats on the water, and colours it orange to red-brown. (Purple is iodine in cyclohexane.)

questions.q: In the reaction \(\mathrm{Br_{2}(aq) + 2I^{-}(aq) \rightarrow 2Br^{-}(aq) + I_{2}(aq)}\), which species is the oxidising agent?
questions.solution: Bromine goes from 0 to −1: it gains electrons, so it is reduced and is the oxidising agent. Iodide goes from −1 to 0: it is oxidised, so it is the reducing agent. (\(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\) and \(\mathrm{I_{2}}\) are products.)

questions.q: Concentrated sulfuric acid is added to solid sodium chloride. Which gas is formed?
questions.solution: \(\mathrm{NaCl + H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow NaHSO_{4} + HCl}\): steamy fumes of hydrogen chloride. This is an acid–base reaction only, because chloride ions are too weak a reducing agent to reduce sulfuric acid. (\(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) forms with bromide, and \(\mathrm{H_{2}S}\) with iodide.)

questions.q: Which product is formed when concentrated sulfuric acid reacts with solid sodium iodide, but not when it reacts with solid sodium bromide?
questions.solution: Iodide is the strongest reducing agent of the halide ions, so it reduces sulfur from +6 all the way to −2, forming \(\mathrm{H_{2}S}\) (and also sulfur, 0). Bromide reduces sulfuric acid only as far as \(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\), +4. (\(\mathrm{SO_{2}}\) forms with both; \(\mathrm{NaHSO_{4}}\) forms with every sodium halide.)

questions.q: In the reaction \(\mathrm{8I^{-} + 8H^{+} + H_{2}SO_{4} \rightarrow 4I_{2} + H_{2}S + 4H_{2}O}\), how many electrons does each sulfur atom gain?
questions.solution: Sulfur has oxidation number +6 in \(\mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}}\) and −2 in \(\mathrm{H_{2}S}\). The change is 6 − (−2) = 8, matching the eight iodide ions that each lose one electron, so each sulfur atom gains 8 electrons. (Treating −2 as +2 leads to 4.)

questions.q: Dilute nitric acid and then silver nitrate solution are added to a solution of sodium bromide. What is seen?
questions.solution: Silver bromide is a cream precipitate: \(\mathrm{Ag^{+}(aq) + Br^{-}(aq) \rightarrow AgBr(s)}\). Silver chloride is white and silver iodide is yellow; silver fluoride is soluble, so fluoride gives no precipitate.

questions.q: A solution gives a precipitate with acidified silver nitrate. The precipitate dissolves in dilute ammonia solution. Which ion was present?
questions.solution: Silver chloride dissolves in dilute ammonia, forming \(\mathrm{[Ag(NH_{3})_{2}]^{+}}\). Silver bromide dissolves only in concentrated ammonia, and silver iodide not at all. (Fluoride gives no precipitate to begin with.)

questions.q: In the test for halide ions, why is the solution acidified with dilute nitric acid rather than dilute hydrochloric acid?

options.A: Nitric acid dissolves the silver carbonate precipitate, but hydrochloric acid does not.
options.B: Hydrochloric acid adds chloride ions, which would give a white precipitate whatever the sample contained.
options.C: Hydrochloric acid oxidises the halide ions to halogens before they can react.
options.D: Nitric acid makes the silver halide precipitates form more slowly, so their colours are easier to see.

questions.solution: The acid is there to remove carbonate and hydroxide ions, which would also precipitate with silver ions. Hydrochloric acid would do that too, but it adds \(\mathrm{Cl^{-}}\) ions, which give white \(\mathrm{AgCl}\) every time. Nitric acid adds only nitrate ions, which never precipitate.

questions.q: Which statement best explains why iodide ions are stronger reducing agents than chloride ions?

options.A: The iodide ion is larger, so its outer electrons are further from the nucleus, more shielded and lost more easily.
options.B: Iodine is more electronegative than chlorine, so iodide ions hold their electrons less strongly.
options.C: The iodide ion has more protons, so it attracts electrons from other species more strongly.
options.D: The iodide ion has a smaller charge than the chloride ion.

questions.solution: A reducing agent loses electrons. The iodide ion has more shells than the chloride ion, so its outer electrons are further from the nucleus and better shielded; they are lost more easily. (Both ions have a 1− charge, and iodine is less electronegative than chlorine, not more.)

questions.q: Chlorine reacts with water: \(\mathrm{Cl_{2} + H_{2}O \rightleftharpoons HCl + HClO}\). What are the oxidation numbers of chlorine in \(\mathrm{HCl}\) and in \(\mathrm{HClO}\)?
questions.solution: In \(\mathrm{HCl}\), H is +1, so Cl is −1. In \(\mathrm{HClO}\), H is +1 and O is −2, so Cl is +1. The chlorine is both reduced (0 to −1) and oxidised (0 to +1): a disproportionation. So the answer is −1 and +1.

questions.q: Which reaction is a disproportionation?
questions.solution: In disproportionation the same element is both oxidised and reduced. In \(\mathrm{Cl_{2} + 2NaOH \rightarrow NaCl + NaClO + H_{2}O}\), chlorine goes from 0 to −1 in \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) and from 0 to +1 in \(\mathrm{NaClO}\). (The displacement and the reaction with sodium are redox, but a different element is oxidised; the sulfuric acid reaction is not redox at all.)

questions.q: Chlorine reacts with hot, concentrated sodium hydroxide: \(\mathrm{3Cl_{2} + 6NaOH \rightarrow 5NaCl + NaClO_{3} + 3H_{2}O}\). What is the oxidation number of chlorine in \(\mathrm{NaClO_{3}}\)?
questions.solution: Na is +1 and each O is −2, so Cl + 1 − 6 = 0, and Cl = +5. Five chlorine atoms each gain one electron (to −1) and one loses five electrons (to +5), so the electrons balance. (The +1 state is chlorate(I), formed with cold, dilute alkali.)

questions.q: Chlorine is toxic. Why is it still added to drinking water?

options.A: It kills disease-causing bacteria, and at the low concentrations used the health benefits outweigh the risks.
options.B: It removes calcium and magnesium ions, which make the water hard.
options.C: It reacts with the water to form chloride ions, which are needed in the diet.
options.D: It removes dissolved fluoride ions, which damage teeth.

questions.solution: Chlorine and the chloric(I) acid it forms kill bacteria that cause diseases such as cholera and typhoid. The concentration used is very low, so the benefit to public health far outweighs the small risk from its toxicity or from chlorinated by-products.

questions.q: Chlorine water is left in bright sunlight and a gas is slowly given off. Which gas is it?
questions.solution: In sunlight chlorine reacts with water to give chloride ions and oxygen: \(\mathrm{2Cl_{2} + 2H_{2}O \rightarrow 4HCl + O_{2}}\). The hydrogen chloride stays dissolved as hydrochloric acid, so the gas given off is oxygen.

questions.q: Using trends in Group 7, which prediction about astatine is most likely to be correct?

options.A: Astatine displaces iodine from aqueous potassium iodide.
options.B: Astatine is a gas at room temperature.
options.C: The astatide ion, \(\mathrm{At^{-}}\), is a weaker reducing agent than the iodide ion.
options.D: Silver astatide is a precipitate that does not dissolve in concentrated ammonia solution.

questions.solution: Silver halides become less soluble in ammonia down the group: \(\mathrm{AgI}\) does not dissolve even in concentrated ammonia, so \(\mathrm{AgAt}\) will not either. Astatine is the weakest oxidising agent, so it cannot displace iodine; it would be a dark solid; and \(\mathrm{At^{-}}\) would be the strongest reducing halide ion.

questions.q: Hydrogen chloride gas from one bottle meets ammonia gas from another. What is seen?

options.C: Dense white smoke of ammonium chloride

questions.solution: The two gases react to form solid ammonium chloride as a dense white smoke: \(\mathrm{NH_{3}(g) + HCl(g) \rightarrow NH_{4}Cl(s)}\). Hydrogen chloride acts as an acid, giving a proton to ammonia; no redox takes place.
